posts.author: Ed Wesly
posts.content_md:
I was there on July 12th with Hans Bjelkhagen, and Loren looked a bit on the frail side. In fact, when I hugged her goodbye (and she must have liked it, as she made me do it 3 times, either that or she forgot that I had already hugged her!) I could feel her skeleton through her clothes.

When Hans introduced himself to her, she first gave him a blank look, then he introduced himself again, and she said, "Oh, I know a Hans Bjelkhagen!" and when Hans told her the 3rd time that he was Hans, she finally recognized him.

She finally recognized me, and we had a cordial time. She is in her 80's, so it is unclear how long she can keep going. She got swindled out of over a half a million bucks, search her name at the Chicago Sun-Times and Tribune pages for the details, and the last I know she was appealing the decision. (I myself **don't** feel sorry for her, as I hold her responsible for the death of 3 or 4 people as a result of her inactions. Karma coming 'round full circle.)

That's the latest that I know, but a lot can happen in a month. I wouldn't necessarily take a down web site as an indicator of the place being closed. Nor her not answering the phone. But it could be annoying to make the trip into town and find it not open. But then again, you can come visit me!

this is all ive been able to read..........

CHICAGO (AP) -- Illinois Treasurer Alexi Giannoulias testified Tuesday in Cook County Circuit Court in defense of a $1 million loan his family's bank made in 2002 to an elderly woman who could now lose her home. 

Broadway Bank officials made the loan to Loren Billings despite what Billings' son claims were indications she was mentally incompetent and being swindled by three business partners. Terrence Kasprazak sued the bank last year. 

Giannoulias, a bank employee in 2002, testified that when he met with Billings, she seemed competent and had good credit. He admitted he had concerns about her partners, so he wrote Billings a letter in 2002 that warned her about their poor credit and questionable pasts. 

After the loan was made in 2002, Billings' partners quickly bilked her of most of the loan. 

The civil trial began Tuesday before Judge Sophia Hall without a jury.
